title: From Toddy Shops to Tribeca: How Kerala Became America's Most Wanted Regional Cuisine
excerpt: With three new Manhattan restaurants, a Michelin star in San Francisco, and a Datassential nod as the 'Cuisine to Know for 2026,' Kerala's coconut-laced cooking has arrived on the global stage.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • Kerala cuisine is now America's most sought-after regional Indian food.
  • 39% of US consumers are interested in trying Keralan dishes.
  • Three new Keralan restaurants opened in Manhattan, showcasing diverse culinary traditions.
  • Michelin-starred restaurants are elevating Keralan cuisine's status in the US.
  • A new generation of chefs is redefining Keralan food in America.

In the sprawling universe of Indian cuisine in America, one state — population 35 million, about the size of Switzerland — is having a moment that no one predicted and everyone is now scrambling to understand. Kerala, India's southwestern spice coast, has gone from a culinary afterthought in the American dining scene to its most coveted regional cuisine in less than two years. The numbers, the restaurants, and the awards are all pointing in the same direction. ## The Data Says Kerala Datassential, the Chicago-based food intelligence firm that predicts dining trends before they hit menus, named Keralan food its "Cuisine to Know for 2026." The designation is not handed out casually — it means the data shows Keralan concepts appearing on American menus at a statistically significant rate, with enough consumer pull to sustain growth. Thirty-nine per cent of US consumers say they are interested in trying Keralan cuisine, according to Datassential's findings. That is a remarkable figure for a regional Indian cuisine that most Americans could not have placed on a map five years ago. "Keralan concepts are popping up stateside, with a variety of U.S. operators calling out Keralan dishes and beverages on menus," the Datassential report states. "Keralan cuisine is characterised by seafood, rice, coconut, veggie-forward dishes, and spices like curry leaves, turmeric, and asafoetida." ## Three Manhattan Openings, One Message > **""Kerala holds a special place in my heart — its warmth, its people, and of course, its incredible food," said Reena Ninan, the ABC News journalist and entrepreneur, at Chatti's launch."** The most visible evidence of Kerala's rise sits on the island of Manhattan, where three Keralan restaurants have opened in rapid succession. **Chatti**, by Chef Regi Mathew, is the most ambitious. Mathew and his team spent over three years in Kerala before opening, visiting 300 homes and 100 toddy shops, testing 800 recipes, and mastering rare cooking techniques. The restaurant recreates the earthy, communal spirit of Kerala's toddy shops — informal watering holes where locals gather over palm wine and sharply spiced small plates. "Kerala holds a special place in my heart — its warmth, its people, and of course, its incredible food," said Reena Ninan, the ABC News journalist and entrepreneur, at Chatti's launch. "The flavors of Kerala aren't just about spice; they tell stories, carry traditions, and evoke a deep sense of home." **Kidilum**, which draws from the Malabar coast, takes a different approach. Chef Raveendran built the menu around memories of his cousin's tea shop in Kerala, offering a coconut-drenched menu that spans mini steamed idli with podi, nandu crab curry, thalassery biryani with goat, and a tart-hot pork vindaloo that nods to the region's Portuguese trade history. Resy, the reservation platform, has featured the restaurant prominently, describing it as "bringing the Malabar Coast to Manhattan." Meanwhile, established powerhouse **Semma** in Greenwich Village — which won a Michelin star for its South Indian menu — continues to prove that regional Indian cuisines can earn the industry's highest accolades. ## The San Francisco Connection On the West Coast, Michelin-starred chef Srijith Gopinathan — born in Kerala, raised in Tamil Nadu — has built his Cal-India Collective around the flavours of coastal South India. His restaurant Copra, in San Francisco's Fillmore district, centres on the spices, techniques and seafood traditions of Kerala, Tamil Nadu and Sri Lanka. The collective, which also includes Ettan, Eylan, and Little Blue Door across Palo Alto, Menlo Park and Los Altos, was nominated as a finalist for the 2026 James Beard Outstanding Restaurateur Award — alongside the Chai Pani Restaurant Group, another Indian-rooted operation. "Copra does not reach for Indian cuisine as a broad category, but for the specific coastal states where Gopinathan learned to cook," noted food publication Food Drink Life. This hyper-regional approach is precisely what makes Keralan cuisine resonate: it offers specificity in a dining landscape drowning in vague "Indian fusion."
Keralan Cuisine Highlights
›Keralan cuisine features seafood, rice, and coconut-based dishes.
›New chefs are bringing personal storytelling to their cooking.
›Keralan food is gaining recognition alongside other global cuisines.
›The cuisine reflects a blend of Christian and Muslim culinary traditions.
## Why Kerala, Why Now Several forces have converged. The global wellness movement has amplified interest in coconut-based cooking, plant-forward meals, and anti-inflammatory spices — all staples of Keralan food. The state's Christian and Muslim communities bring a seafood-and-meat-heavy repertoire that challenges the vegetarian stereotype that often limits how Americans perceive Indian cuisine. There is also a generational shift at work. A new cohort of Malayali chefs — many of them trained in the Middle East and Europe before coming to the US — are bringing technical sophistication and personal storytelling to their cooking, refusing to flatten their cuisine into a generic "curry" category. ## What It Means for the Diaspora For the estimated 500,000 Malayalis in the United States, the Kerala dining boom is deeply personal. For decades, Keralan food was something you ate at home, at temple events, or at the handful of Kerala restaurants scattered across New Jersey and Houston. It was rarely celebrated in the mainstream press, and almost never at the Michelin or James Beard level. That has changed, decisively. Kerala's cuisine is being discussed alongside Japanese, Mexican and Italian as a regional tradition worthy of deep exploration — not a subset of "Indian" that gets flattened into tikka masala and naan. ## What's Next Industry observers expect more Keralan concepts to emerge, particularly in metro areas with large Malayali populations — Houston, Dallas, Chicago, the Bay Area, and the greater New York tri-state area. The heritage cuisine trend, which prizes specificity over fusion, shows no signs of slowing: three of the five finalists for the 2026 James Beard Outstanding Restaurateur Award are building from a named cultural address. As Datassential's data suggests, Americans are not just ready for Indian food anymore. They are ready for Keralan food, Goan food, Nagaland food — the actual India, not the sanitised export version. And Kerala got there first.
